chapters.title: Week 1 — Business, Law, Morality & Ethics
chapters.description: Current 2026–27 foundations, corporate purpose and ethical responsibility.

questions.stem: A retailer complies with consumer law but conceals an avoidable social harm. Why is further ethical analysis still relevant?

options.text: Legal compliance is a minimum standard, not a complete moral judgement
Ethical duties apply only when a court finds fraud
Consumer demand makes every lawful choice ethical
Compliance establishes that no values conflict

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes legal minimums from questions of right and wrong where values conflict.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slides 6, 16

questions.stem: Which activity falls most directly within business ethics?

options.text: Recording the number of suppliers as a purely descriptive fact
Calculating a supplier invoice without evaluating the decision
Examining whether a supplier-selection decision is right or wrong
Listing products without considering any decision or harm

questions.explanation: Business ethics studies morally significant business situations, activities and decisions.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: A manager invokes Friedman to justify deceiving customers for profit. What qualification has the manager omitted?

options.text: Profit-seeking must respect open competition without deception or fraud
Shareholders must approve every individual sale
Managers must prioritise philanthropy over all commercial activity
Profit-seeking is allowed only by non-profit organisations

questions.explanation: Friedman’s stated argument expressly restricts profit-seeking by the rules of the game and the exclusion of deception and fraud.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 9

questions.stem: In Friedman’s shareholder-agency argument, whose agent is the corporate executive primarily?

options.text: The owners of the corporation
Every citizen affected by the industry equally
The executive’s preferred charity
The government’s competition authority

questions.explanation: The executive is described as an employee and agent of the owners, responsible for conducting the business in accordance with their desires.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 10

questions.stem: Which claim accurately represents the ethical problem with treating profit as the only business concern?

options.text: A profitable decision can still impose serious harm on other people
Profit removes the need to examine employee pressure
Only loss-making businesses can cause harm
Profit and ethical conduct cannot coexist

questions.explanation: The need for ethics includes corporate power, stakeholder demands and the personal harm caused by malpractice.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 13

questions.stem: A company has extensive legal advice but employees feel pressured to compromise their standards. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Regulation does not remove every organisational ethical pressure
Employee beliefs are irrelevant whenever lawyers are involved
Legal expertise necessarily prevents misconduct
Pressure to compromise is proof that the law has been broken

questions.explanation: The slides identify pressure on employees as a reason for business ethics despite extensive regulation.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slides 7, 13

questions.stem: Why is corporate lobbying relevant to the case for business ethics?

options.text: Lobbying removes the distinction between laws and values
Businesses can influence democratic processes as well as market outcomes
Lobbying means a company has ceased to pursue profit
Lobbying guarantees that policy benefits all citizens

questions.explanation: The deck highlights business power and its impact on democratic processes; influence must be evaluated rather than presumed beneficial.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slides 13–14

questions.stem: Which statement best fits the deck’s reasoned distinction between morality and ethics?

options.text: Morality includes norms and beliefs about right and wrong; ethics critically examines and applies principles to conduct
Morality excludes social norms; ethics excludes reasoning
Morality is legislation; ethics is private preference only
Morality concerns business only; ethics concerns individuals only

questions.explanation: The Crane and Matten distinction connects morality with norms, values and beliefs and ethics with their reasoned examination.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 21

questions.stem: A defence professional’s personal wish for justice conflicts with the professional relationship owed to a client. What is the central lesson?

options.text: Professional codes always express every personal moral belief
Personal conviction automatically settles professional conduct
Personal moral conviction and professional ethical obligations can conflict
A conflict proves that professional obligations are meaningless

questions.explanation: The example illustrates tension between personal morality and role-based ethical obligations, not a universal permission to breach a code.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 20

questions.stem: Which question most clearly goes beyond asking whether conduct is legal?

options.text: Has the mandatory form been signed?
Which values and stakeholder interests conflict in this decision?
What filing date is recorded by the regulator?
Which statute number appears in the contract?

questions.explanation: Ethical analysis examines competing values, rather than stopping at procedural or legal compliance.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 16

questions.stem: A company faces mistrust even though it has not been convicted of an offence. Which reason for business ethics applies most directly?

options.text: The trust deficit between businesses and those affected by them
The need to make all firms adopt one product price
The assumption that reputation proves legal guilt
The absence of any relevant social expectations

questions.explanation: The deck identifies a trust deficit as a reason for ethical reflection; mistrust is not itself proof of an offence.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 13

questions.stem: Why do supplier working conditions remain relevant to a buyer’s ethical decisions?

options.text: A signed purchase order proves all supplier practices are acceptable
Supplier treatment matters only when prices rise
Ethical concerns end at the buyer’s legal ownership boundary
Stakeholders increasingly expect businesses to consider supplier treatment

questions.explanation: The slides cite care for suppliers and Fairtrade expectations as part of the growing demands on business.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 13

questions.stem: Which response best recognises the limits of extensive business regulation?

options.text: Assume all unregulated actions are morally acceptable
Treat professional standards as guarantees of good intentions
Check the rules, then assess harms and values not fully settled by them
Replace every law with the manager’s personal preferences

questions.explanation: The deck’s law–ethics distinction requires judgement beyond a legal minimum, without abandoning law.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slides 7, 16

questions.stem: Friedman argues that individuals may spend their own money on social causes. What objection is this intended to raise about executives?

options.text: Executives should not automatically use owners' resources for their own preferred causes
Employees should be prevented from charitable giving
Customers must donate whenever a firm makes a profit
Profitable firms cannot provide any benefit to society

questions.explanation: The agency argument distinguishes an executive’s corporate responsibility from an individual’s choice to spend personal resources.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 10

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly explains why values can conflict in business?

options.text: A decision protects jobs but exposes another group to avoidable harm
A manager reads a price before making any decision
A spreadsheet lists the same date in two cells
A firm changes its logo without affecting anyone’s interests

questions.explanation: Ethical dilemmas can involve competing legitimate interests; they are not resolved merely by recording facts.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 1 deck; slide 16

chapters.title: Week 2 — Behaviour, Bias & Leadership
chapters.description: Current 2026–27 situational pressures, moral mechanisms and leadership risks.

questions.stem: An employee approves a harmful action because a senior manager ordered it. Which mechanism best fits?

options.text: False consensus effect
Moral compensation
Conformity with peers
Obedience to authority

questions.explanation: The deck links obedience to authority with following authoritative direction despite ethical concerns.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 14

questions.stem: A new employee accepts dubious practices because everyone in the team does them. Which bias is most direct?

options.text: Instant-entitlement bias
Moral compensation
Loss aversion
Conformity bias

questions.explanation: Conformity involves taking cues from the group and fitting in with its behaviour.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 14

questions.stem: A worker takes an unusually large ethical risk to avoid losing an existing job. Which mechanism best fits?

options.text: Moral licensing
Loss aversion
False consensus
Conceptual disagreement

questions.explanation: The slides distinguish risk-taking to avoid a loss from risk-taking to obtain an equivalent gain.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 14

questions.stem: A manager credits personal skill for success but blames colleagues and circumstances for failure. What is this?

options.text: Moral compensation
Rule utilitarianism
Discourse ethics
Self-serving bias

questions.explanation: Self-serving bias protects self-image through asymmetric explanations of success and failure.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 14

questions.stem: After donating to charity, a buyer feels entitled to overlook a supplier’s exploitation. Which mechanism is illustrated?

options.text: False consensus effect
Fair equality of opportunity
Moral compensation
Moral licensing

questions.explanation: Moral licensing treats past good deeds as credit that permits later questionable conduct.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 17

questions.stem: After acting unfairly, an employee donates to a cause to restore a sense of moral balance. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: Moral licensing
Instant-entitlement bias
Moral compensation
Conformity bias

questions.explanation: Compensation seeks to make up perceived moral credit; licensing spends credit already accumulated.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 17

questions.stem: A decision is made impulsively, then defended with elaborate ethical arguments. Which process best fits?

options.text: Original-position reasoning
Self-serving attribution of success
Rule utilitarianism
Moral rationalisation

questions.explanation: The deck warns that reasoning may justify a decision already made automatically or emotionally.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slides 17, 21

questions.stem: A supervisor explains misconduct solely as evidence that an employee is a bad person, ignoring intense organisational pressure. Which error is most direct?

options.text: False consensus effect
Loss aversion
Moral licensing
Fundamental attribution error

questions.explanation: The error overemphasises disposition while underestimating situational influences.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 17

questions.stem: A leader assumes most people share their opinions without checking. What is this?

options.text: False consensus effect
Fair opportunity
Kantian universalisation
Moral compensation

questions.explanation: False consensus overestimates the prevalence of one’s own attitudes and beliefs.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 17

questions.stem: Two groups inspect the same mixed evidence and each becomes more convinced of its original position. Which lesson fits the capital-punishment example?

options.text: Both groups must have received different studies
Biased evaluation of evidence can increase polarisation
Identical evidence always produces agreement
Exposure to evidence removes all self-serving bias

questions.explanation: The slides describe favouring belief-consistent evidence, producing polarisation rather than convergence.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 16

questions.stem: Why can calling a bribe a facilitation payment matter ethically?

options.text: A softer label necessarily changes the legal status
The label proves that no one is harmed
Technical terminology eliminates personal responsibility
Euphemistic language can obscure the moral character of an action

questions.explanation: The deck identifies language as one way workplace conduct can become ethically distanced.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 13

questions.stem: How can bureaucracy contribute to unethical conduct?

options.text: It can distance employees from the people affected by their actions
It guarantees shared moral standards
It removes organisational roles and incentives
It ensures employees see every consequence directly

questions.explanation: Bureaucratic distance is one of the situational influences listed in the slides.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 13

questions.stem: A person given a leadership role takes more than their share of goods. Which leadership risk is most direct?

options.text: Moral compensation
False consensus effect
Instant-entitlement bias
Moral licensing

questions.explanation: The deck uses allocation experiments to illustrate entitlement associated with leadership roles.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 20

questions.stem: A powerful leader believes ordinary rules apply to others but that they can manipulate outcomes to escape consequences. Which concept fits?

options.text: The harm principle
Bathsheba syndrome
The difference principle
Conformity bias

questions.explanation: The deck describes a belief in personal exemption and the ability to manipulate consequences.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slide 20

questions.stem: Why should a strong self-image as a good person not replace scrutiny of workplace behaviour?

options.text: Ethical character cannot be influenced by a situation
Only people with a negative self-image rationalise decisions
Multiple pressures and biases can still shape conduct
A positive self-image proves all actions are moral

questions.explanation: The slides contrast favourable self-ratings with situational, emotional and organisational influences on actual behaviour.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 2 deck; slides 11, 13–17

chapters.title: Week 3 — Business Impacts & Evidence
chapters.description: Current-year global-business examples, distribution, resources and evidence interpretation.

questions.stem: A phone manufacturer buys through several intermediaries. What ethical issue does the Rubaya coltan example highlight?

options.text: Every smartphone has been proved to contain ore from that mine
Only the final assembly factory can raise an ethical issue
Upstream mineral sourcing can connect ordinary products with conflict financing and worker hardship
Consumer demand automatically prevents exploitation

questions.explanation: The supplied article traces coltan extraction and conflict-related control; it does not establish the origin of every product.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Rubaya coltan article

questions.stem: Why should a buyer investigate conditions beyond its immediate supplier in a mineral supply chain?

options.text: An intermediary guarantees the absence of conflict financing
Harm can occur upstream even when the immediate transaction appears routine
Supply-chain distance means upstream harms cannot matter
A low purchase price proves workers consented freely

questions.explanation: The Rubaya example shows that extraction conditions and financing can be hidden several steps before final manufacturing.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Rubaya coltan article

questions.stem: What does comparing food waste with unmet food needs most directly invite us to examine?

options.text: Whether waste proves no one lacks food
Allocation and distribution, not just total production
Whether all food can be moved at zero cost
Whether higher prices always eliminate hunger

questions.explanation: The juxtaposition raises questions about how available resources are used and distributed, without settling logistics or causation.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; food-waste reports

questions.stem: Luxury travel and severe deprivation are shown alongside each other. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Total wealth or consumption does not reveal how benefits are distributed
Aggregate prosperity guarantees everyone’s needs are met
Every luxury purchase has been proved to cause a particular person’s poverty
All expensive services are illegal

questions.explanation: Contrasting consumption levels invites distributional analysis, not an automatic causal judgement about each purchase.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; luxury and deprivation examples

questions.stem: Why is access to scarce water a business-ethics issue in the Nuevo Leon example?

options.text: A commercial allocation guarantees equal access
Industrial use and household needs compete for a limited resource
Water use affects firms but cannot affect communities
The highest-paying user is automatically morally entitled to all supply

questions.explanation: The report highlights tensions between companies' water use and residents' access during drought.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Nuevo Leon water report

questions.stem: Which is the best distinction between an ocean-plastic stock and an annual pollution flow?

options.text: A stock is always measured per year; a flow has no time dimension
A stock measures only visible floating plastic
Both quantities necessarily describe the same year’s input
A stock is an accumulated amount; a flow is an amount entering over a stated period

questions.explanation: The deck contains accumulated ocean-floor estimates and annual-entry estimates; their units and time meanings differ.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; ocean-plastic report

questions.stem: A report estimates plastic on the ocean floor. Why should it not be treated as an estimate of plastic entering the sea this year?

options.text: Ocean-floor plastic cannot persist across years
All pollution reports use identical measures
The location of plastic supplies its date of entry
Accumulated stock and annual inflow measure different things

questions.explanation: The stock–flow distinction prevents comparing unlike quantities as if they were equivalent.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; ocean-plastic report

questions.stem: What ethical issue is raised by lobbying against a proposed disposable-cup levy?

options.text: A proposed levy and an enacted levy are the same
Lobbying establishes that environmental costs do not exist
Opposition to a proposal proves the company broke an enacted law
Commercial interests may conflict with environmental-policy objectives

questions.explanation: The Costa example concerns influence over a policy proposal, not proof of non-compliance with an enacted levy.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Costa cup-levy report

questions.stem: A rainforest can shift towards a different ecosystem after sufficient stress. Which idea does the Amazon example illustrate?

options.text: Proof that business activity has no ecological effects
A guarantee that every damaged forest recovers immediately
A rule that all environmental change is linear
An environmental tipping point rather than necessarily a smooth reversible change

questions.explanation: The report discusses a rainforest-to-savannah shift and the risks of threshold effects.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Amazon tipping-point report

questions.stem: How should the Purdue bankruptcy article’s claims about promotion and addiction risk be represented?

options.text: As a complete current legal verdict from every jurisdiction
As proof that all medicines are addictive
As allegations described in a dated report unless their later resolution is separately verified
As evidence that bankruptcy itself determines moral innocence

questions.explanation: The deck’s 2019 article reports lawsuits and allegations; it does not provide every later outcome.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; Purdue bankruptcy report

questions.stem: The technology-company report discusses market dominance and onerous terms. What ethical issue is central?

options.text: Whether any large firm is automatically a monopoly in every market
How concentrated commercial power affects dependent people and businesses
Whether profitability proves that every contract is fair
Whether popular products remove governance concerns

questions.explanation: The report raises concerns about fees, terms, data and the exercise of platform power.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; 2020 technology-company report

questions.stem: A customer buys an expensive trip but service failures ruin the planned experience. What does this illustrate?

options.text: A transaction is ethical whenever payment was accepted
Price alone guarantees the promised experience
Business failures can impose personal costs beyond the amount paid
Personal distress is unrelated to commercial performance

questions.explanation: The travel examples show how organisational service failures affect people’s plans and experiences.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; travel-service failures

questions.stem: Why should conflicting conflict-death estimates not be combined into one apparently precise figure?

options.text: A smaller estimate must be the official final count
Averaging different estimates always removes uncertainty
Their sources, definitions and coverage may not be comparable
A larger estimate is automatically more reliable

questions.explanation: The supplied Week 3 material contains conflicting estimates; ethical use of evidence requires preserving uncertainty.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; conflict and famine material

questions.stem: A crime chart and a public-perception chart point in different directions. What should an analyst do?

options.text: Assume the charts must use identical units
Discard the measured series because perceptions are real feelings
Compare definitions, time periods and evidence before equating perception with measured change
Treat perceived direction as a verified crime count

questions.explanation: The deck contrasts perception and data; they should be assessed as different forms of evidence.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; perception-versus-reality examples

questions.stem: What is the most defensible way to use a historical statistic in a current ethical discussion?

options.text: Remove its date to make the comparison easier
Assume every statistic in a current deck was measured this year
Treat all dated estimates as irrelevant
Identify its date and measure, then avoid presenting it as a newly verified current figure

questions.explanation: The current deck incorporates dated articles and estimates; teaching-year status does not update each statistic’s reference period.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 3 PDF; dated reports throughout the PDF

chapters.title: Week 4.1 — Ethical Approaches & Frameworks
chapters.description: Descriptive, conceptual and normative ethics; standards, judgements and theory families.

questions.stem: A researcher records how often firms conceal product defects without judging whether they should. Which approach is this?

options.text: Normative ethics
Kantian ethics
Virtue ethics
Descriptive ethics

questions.explanation: Descriptive ethics studies what is actually being done.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: A team asks exactly what responsibility means when applied to a corporation. Which approach is most direct?

options.text: Conceptual ethics
Act utilitarianism
Descriptive ethics
Enlightened egoism

questions.explanation: Conceptual ethics analyses morally important terms and their meaning.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: A manager asks whether a firm ought to stop a discriminatory practice. Which approach is this?

options.text: A market-share calculation
A purely statistical description
Normative ethics
Descriptive ethics

questions.explanation: Normative ethics asks what ought to be done.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: Which statement represents moral absolutism as introduced in the slides?

options.text: Right and wrong have objective qualities that can be assessed rationally
Moral questions are only descriptions of sales figures
Whatever is widespread is morally right
Each decision-maker’s immediate desire settles morality

questions.explanation: Absolutism holds that right and wrong can be objectively judged.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Why does widespread local corruption not by itself establish its ethical acceptability?

options.text: A common practice is not automatically a justified moral standard
Popularity is always the strongest moral proof
Ethics cannot assess culturally common practices
Only uncommon conduct can be unethical

questions.explanation: The slides explicitly warn against treating prevalence as moral justification.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Two managers agree that avoidable harm should be prevented but disagree about whether an activity causes harm. What differs most directly?

options.text: Their view that all harms are irrelevant
Their shared commitment to avoiding harm
Their agreement about the evidence
Their factual judgement rather than necessarily their moral standard

questions.explanation: The slides distinguish disagreement about standards from disagreement about the facts informing judgement.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Two colleagues agree on a fairness principle but prefer different ways to implement it. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Agreement on a standard does not guarantee agreement on its application
Implementation choices are never ethical questions
Only one colleague can understand the word fairness
They necessarily hold opposite moral standards

questions.explanation: People can share a moral standard and disagree about how to achieve it.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Which feature is central to consequentialist evaluation?

options.text: Character without any attention to a decision
The outcomes of available actions
Compliance with duty regardless of outcome
The actor’s job title alone

questions.explanation: Consequentialist theories focus on consequences.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: What distinguishes egoism from utilitarianism within consequentialism?

options.text: Egoism focuses on the decision-maker’s interests; utilitarianism on wider social outcomes
Both theories require the same personal-benefit measure
Egoism always ignores outcomes; utilitarianism ignores society
Egoism is exclusively about duties; utilitarianism exclusively about character

questions.explanation: The deck contrasts whose outcomes guide the judgement.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: Which question is most directly deontological?

options.text: What duty must be upheld even if violating it would bring benefits?
Which habit builds market share fastest?
Which action gives the highest total measured utility?
Which action maximises my immediate enjoyment?

questions.explanation: Deontological theories centre duties, rights and universal law.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: Which question is most directly associated with virtue ethics?

options.text: What kind of character and habitual conduct should this person cultivate?
Which option maximises one transaction’s revenue?
Which regulation has the shortest title?
Which action has the largest numerical benefit only?

questions.explanation: Virtue ethics focuses on character rather than only outcomes or individual rules.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: Two actions have different intentions and different unintended results. What should a careful ethical comparison distinguish?

options.text: Intention, action and outcome
Only the number of witnesses
Only the actor’s income
Only the final outcome in every theory

questions.explanation: The opening dilemma separates motivations, conduct and consequences rather than assuming one framework settles every judgement.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 2

questions.stem: A normative business framework assumes people are opportunistic. Why should that assumption be made explicit?

options.text: Every theory makes identical assumptions about people
Assumptions are irrelevant to ethical recommendations
Opportunism is proved universal by the existence of a framework
The assumed account of human behaviour influences the framework’s recommendations

questions.explanation: The deck notes that normative approaches rest on specific assumptions about the world and human nature.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 5

questions.stem: Which statement best separates an observation from a prescription?

options.text: Most firms use this practice describes behaviour; firms ought to use it makes a normative judgement
Both statements merely count behaviour
Only the first statement makes a moral prescription
Neither statement can be examined ethically

questions.explanation: What is being done and what ought to be done are different questions.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: Why might a multinational’s consistent global code face challenges from moral relativism?

options.text: Relativism proves that all corporate codes are illegal
Consistency eliminates all need for judgement
Locally formed moral norms may conflict with a uniform organisational standard
Every culture necessarily has identical norms

questions.explanation: The slides discuss cultural values alongside multinationals' attempts to use consistent codes.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 1 deck; slide 4

chapters.title: Week 4.2 — Utilitarianism
chapters.description: Aggregate consequences, act/rule distinctions, Bentham, Mill and limitations.

questions.stem: Which criterion best captures utilitarian choice between alternatives?

options.text: Choose the action that benefits only the decision-maker
Choose the action that best expresses personal loyalty only
Choose the available action with at least as favourable a balance of value over disvalue as the others
Choose the oldest organisational rule regardless of outcomes

questions.explanation: The deck’s definition compares the balance of benefits and harms across available actions.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: A manager calculates the consequences of one particular proposed decision. Which utilitarian approach fits?

options.text: Virtue ethics
Kantian duty ethics
Rule utilitarianism
Act utilitarianism

questions.explanation: Act utilitarianism evaluates a particular case.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: A firm assesses the long-run consequences of consistently following a general policy. Which approach fits?

options.text: Rights-based non-interference alone
Act utilitarianism limited to one decision
Rule utilitarianism
Immediate egoism

questions.explanation: Rule utilitarianism considers consequences across cases and over time.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: A project creates jobs but damages the local environment. What does utilitarian evaluation require?

options.text: Count jobs and ignore every environmental effect
Compare benefits and harms, including those affecting different groups
Treat profit as identical to total social utility
Refuse to consider outcomes because only duties matter

questions.explanation: The deck uses a mining project to illustrate competing consequences in a cost–benefit-style analysis.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Why is a high total benefit not enough to dismiss objections by a harmed minority?

options.text: Only financial shareholders can bear costs
Minority interests cannot enter utilitarian calculations
A majority benefit proves nobody experiences harm
Aggregate benefit can conceal who bears the costs

questions.explanation: The slides identify minority burdens and the distribution of costs as difficulties for utilitarian analysis.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: What is a key challenge in quantifying utility for a business decision?

options.text: Only benefits require measurement, not harms
Every consequence already has one objective market price
Subjective judgement is impossible in analysis
Different harms and benefits can be difficult to measure and compare

questions.explanation: The deck raises quantification and analyst subjectivity as problems.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: Which focus is associated with Bentham’s approach in the deck?

options.text: The executive’s duty to owners alone
The unconditional duty to follow a maxim
Pleasure and pain assessed through a hedonic calculus
Habitual virtues independent of consequences

questions.explanation: Bentham’s account seeks a quantifiable balance of pleasure and pain.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 5

questions.stem: What does Bentham’s consequentialist emphasis place above the actor’s moral character?

options.text: The actor’s social status
The age of the organisation
The actor’s profession
The consequences of the action

questions.explanation: The slides distinguish consequences from character, motivation and circumstances in presenting Bentham.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 5

questions.stem: Which criticism targets an overly mechanistic utilitarian approach?

options.text: It always refuses to compare any outcomes
It requires all choices to follow one religious code
It can reduce people to utility measures and omit natural rights
It ignores every majority benefit by definition

questions.explanation: The listed criticisms include treating people as utility functions and failing to protect natural rights.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 5

questions.stem: How does the deck characterise Mill’s departure from a purely mechanistic approach?

options.text: Exclusive pursuit of corporate shareholders' immediate profit
Greater concern for individual freedom, flourishing and minority protection
Rejection of every consequence-based consideration
A claim that humans should be managed exactly like machines

questions.explanation: Mill sought to combine utilitarian reasoning with freedom and protections for individuals.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: According to Mill’s harm principle, what justifies imposing power on an individual against their will?

options.text: Making the individual agree with the majority
Improving that individual’s welfare alone in every case
Increasing the decision-maker’s convenience
Preventing harm to other people

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes preventing harm to others from acting only for the individual’s own good.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 4 Part 2 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: Why can the harm principle still generate disagreement?

options.text: It says every disliked choice is harmful to others
It automatically resolves all emotional and cognitive harms
Harm can be difficult to define objectively in contested cases
It requires no interpretation of any facts

questions.stem: Which statement represents a normative stakeholder approach?

options.text: Ethical worth is identical to bargaining power
Stakeholder interests deserve ethical consideration in their own right
Stakeholders matter only if they can raise quarterly profits
Stakeholder mapping is only a list of names

questions.explanation: Normative analysis concerns why stakeholder interests ought to matter, not merely whether consideration is profitable.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: In the lecture’s stakeholder categories, which group is an example of enabling stakeholders?

options.text: Customers
Professional peer associations
Diffuse public campaign groups
Regulators

questions.explanation: The enabling category includes actors such as regulators, shareholders and the board.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: In the lecture’s stakeholder categories, employees, suppliers and customers are primarily examples of which category?

options.text: Enabling only
Normative only
Diffused only
Functional

questions.explanation: Functional stakeholders participate in the inputs and outputs of business activity.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Why should the label normative stakeholder category not be confused with normative stakeholder theory?

options.text: Both labels mean only shareholders
The category identifies everyone with low interest
The theory is simply a list of media outlets
The category classifies groups such as peer associations; the theory concerns ethical justification

questions.explanation: The lecture uses normative in two distinct classification contexts.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A stakeholder has high power and high interest in a project. What is the usual power–interest matrix approach?

options.text: Treat as automatically irrelevant
Manage closely
Monitor with minimal engagement only
Keep uninformed

questions.explanation: High-power, high-interest stakeholders generally require close management and engagement.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A stakeholder has high power but currently low interest. What approach fits the power–interest matrix?

options.text: Use the low-power, high-interest strategy without considering their power
Keep satisfied
Ignore completely
Assume they have no influence

questions.explanation: The matrix recommends keeping high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A community group has low formal power but high interest. What approach fits the matrix while respecting stakeholder ethics?

options.text: Keep informed and consider its interests rather than dismissing them
Ignore it because low power means no moral worth
Transfer its interests to shareholders without consultation
Assume it must control every decision

questions.explanation: The usual strategy is to keep it informed; power is not a measure of intrinsic ethical worth.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Why should a stakeholder priority map be revisited rather than treated as permanent?

options.text: Only the number of shares can ever change priority
Power, interest and urgency can change as circumstances develop
All stakeholder interests disappear after the first meeting
The map guarantees that no conflict can arise

questions.explanation: Stakeholder management is dynamic; an initial assessment can become outdated.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

chapters.title: Week 6.2 — Governance & Protected Disclosures
chapters.description: Lecture 6: board and management roles, workplace-resolution bodies and careful recognition of protected disclosures.

questions.stem: Which distinction best describes the board and CEO roles presented in governance teaching?

options.text: The board provides direction and oversight; the CEO leads implementation
The CEO alone sets every governance constraint and oversees themselves
The CEO provides independent oversight of the board while the board handles daily operations
The board and CEO have no distinguishable responsibilities

questions.explanation: Governance separates strategic direction and oversight from day-to-day executive implementation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does separate legal personality mean for an incorporated company?

options.text: The company and every shareholder are always the same legal person
The company has legal personality only while its original members remain
Every employee becomes personally identical to the company
The company is a legal entity distinct from its members

questions.explanation: Separate personality distinguishes the corporate entity from the people involved in it.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does perpetual succession describe in corporate characteristics?

options.text: The original shareholders must remain for the company to continue
Any change in shareholders automatically ends the company
The company can never be wound up
The company can continue despite changes in its membership

questions.explanation: Changes among members do not by themselves end the company’s existence; this does not mean it can never be dissolved.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which description best fits the basic limited-liability characteristic taught for shareholders?

options.text: All shareholders must personally pay every corporate liability without limit
Shareholder exposure is generally limited by their investment or unpaid amount on shares, rather than every corporate debt automatically becoming a personal debt
Shareholders can never lose their investment
Company debts cease to exist when shares are issued

questions.explanation: Limited liability concerns shareholder exposure; it does not mean the business has no debts or risks.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the lecture’s business-judgement discussion?

options.text: Every decision must maximise this week’s revenue
Directors are prohibited from considering any affected community
Good-faith managerial discretion can allow consideration of business context beyond immediate profit
Managers have unrestricted immunity for fraud

questions.explanation: The teaching examples challenge an absolute profit-only reading; discretion is not unlimited or a defence of fraud.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: How should the US corporate-purpose cases discussed in the lecture be used in an Irish-focused ethics question bank?

options.text: As guarantees that every manager will win any lawsuit
As teaching examples illustrating tensions, not as automatic statements of Irish law
As legislation that directly replaces all Irish company law
As proof that every corporation must ignore stakeholders

questions.explanation: The cases support conceptual discussion; jurisdiction-specific legal claims need separate verification.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the range of Workplace Relations Commission functions discussed in the lecture?

options.text: It includes advisory, inspection, mediation and adjudication functions
It offers mediation but has no adjudication function
It adjudicates disputes but has no inspection function
It deals only with employer complaints and not employee complaints

questions.explanation: The WRC has several functions, not just one dispute-resolution role.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which distinction matches the lecture’s Labour Court discussion?

options.text: Every Labour Court output is an identical non-binding suggestion
Every industrial-relations recommendation is automatically a criminal conviction
Industrial-relations recommendations and rights appeals have identical legal effects
Employment-rights appeal determinations and industrial-relations recommendations have different legal effects

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes binding employment-rights appeal determinations from non-binding industrial-relations recommendations.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which feature is central to recognising a potential protected disclosure in the lecture?

options.text: A reasonable belief in relevant wrongdoing encountered in a work-related context
Conclusive proof of every allegation before any report can be made
Any disagreement about personal taste unrelated to work
A personal financial interest in the reported outcome

questions.explanation: Reasonable belief and work-related wrongdoing are key; certainty of the final outcome is not required at the initial report stage.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: A worker reasonably believes a work practice is endangering safety and uses an appropriate reporting channel. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: It is automatically false if management disagrees
It may be a relevant wrongdoing report even before final investigation establishes every fact
It cannot be relevant unless an injury has already occurred
It can be relevant only if the worker personally suffered an injury

questions.explanation: The lecture includes safety risks and wrongdoing that may be occurring or likely to occur; the report is not a final finding.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: A complaint concerns only a personal interpersonal disagreement and alleges no relevant wrongdoing. Which route generally fits the distinction taught?

options.text: An ordinary grievance route rather than automatically treating it as a protected disclosure
Automatic classification as public-funds fraud
A requirement to report it to an unrelated regulator
Ignoring all workplace complaint procedures

questions.explanation: A purely interpersonal grievance is distinguished from relevant wrongdoing; mixed cases still need careful assessment.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What should be checked before using an external prescribed reporting body?

options.text: Whether the reporter can publish every detail publicly first
Whether the body can guarantee a particular remedy in advance
Whether the alleged wrongdoing falls within that body’s remit
Whether the body is the most famous organisation available

questions.explanation: The appropriate external channel depends on the subject and remit, rather than choosing an arbitrary recipient.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does a prima facie assessment of a report establish?

options.text: A provisional initial basis for considering the case, not a final finding that wrongdoing is proved
An automatic final criminal conviction
That no investigation is needed
That confidentiality removes the need to assess the report

questions.explanation: The initial assessment is preliminary and must not be confused with a completed determination.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Why distinguish a reasonably mistaken report from a knowingly false allegation?

options.text: Reasonable belief is not the same as deliberate fabrication
Every mistaken detail proves deliberate dishonesty
Only reports supported by a final court judgment can be made
A knowingly false allegation becomes reasonable whenever it is repeated

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises the belief basis of a report; an error discovered later is not automatically knowing falsity.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary
